Audrey Whitfield

gap-021 · supplement · fictional age 16

Written life first, then interpreted by a separate response author without the engine or results. These are synthetic checks. There is no correct career answer key.

Life from age 4 to 16

I know I'm lucky. Everybody reminds me, especially if I complain. I can be lucky and still want to do one thing without explaining it first. I don't know what my favorite subject is. Usually it's whichever teacher makes it clear how to get a good grade. My friends all sound like they have plans, but sometimes I think we're just saying what we said last time.

  • family: Lives with both parents and a younger brother; parents are attentive, busy, and highly involved in choices; conflict over dating and privacy remains unresolved.
  • finances: Affluent household with private tuition, travel, and paid enrichment available.
  • geography: Austin, Texas; family spends part of each summer with relatives in Colorado.
  • cultureLanguages: White American; English at home; nominal church affiliation, most social life through school families.
  • school: Small college-preparatory private high school; consistently good grades with substantial tutoring and scheduling support.
  • accessOpportunities: Extensive organized opportunities and reliable transport, but very little unsupervised exploration or paid work.
  • Age 4–5

    Audrey's days were arranged around preschool, swimming lessons, and appointments written on a kitchen calendar. She liked sticker books and telling adults what her younger brother was doing wrong. Her parents took many photographs and praised her willingness to smile. She enjoyed familiar visitors but became restless on museum trips chosen because adults thought they would be enriching.

  • Age 6–7

    She attended a small private elementary school where most children knew each other outside class. She learned how to follow classroom expectations and earned frequent good-behavior marks. Her mother tried piano lessons, tennis, and a children's art class. Audrey did not hate them, but she rarely asked to continue once the scheduled session ended or the equipment was put away.

  • Age 8–9

    A tutor helped her prepare spelling and math work twice a week. Audrey liked having someone explain exactly what would be assessed. She spent sleepovers making up rankings of favorite outfits and celebrities. A quieter classmate sometimes became the subject of the group's jokes. Audrey usually laughed along and has never considered herself the person who started them.

  • Age 10–11

    Remote school took place in a dedicated room with a reliable laptop. Her parents organized virtual activities when she complained of boredom. Audrey preferred chatting privately with friends while the official activity ran. She became very familiar with the appearance of other families' homes on camera and began noticing which possessions signaled that someone belonged in her social circle.

  • Age 12–13

    She returned to a school that talked frequently about leadership and future applications. Audrey joined clubs her friends joined and accepted a minor title that required almost no work. She received praise for a polished presentation after a tutor helped structure it. She knew the final result looked good but could not say which part she had actually enjoyed producing.

  • Age 14–15

    A relationship with a boy at another school occupied more thought than her classes. Her parents wanted access to her messages after she lied about where a group was meeting. Audrey viewed their response as humiliating; they viewed her refusal to explain as proof of poor judgment. The rules tightened, and she became more skilled at giving technically true, incomplete answers.

  • Age 16

    At sixteen she earns good grades, tracks deadlines carefully, and spends considerable time maintaining group chats and browsing resale clothes. She has no sustained hobby outside those social routines. Her parents discuss selective colleges as a shared family project. Audrey wants to go somewhere they cannot visit without planning, but has not separated that desire from interest in any course of study.

Life now

  • enjoys: Group chats · Resale fashion browsing · Familiar cafés with friends · Planning social outings
  • avoids: Looking inexperienced in public · Activities none of her friends attend · Unstructured reflection assignments
  • activities: School social committees with limited duties · Tutoring · Weekend outings arranged with parental permission
  • demonstratedSkills: Tracks deadlines with calendar support · Coordinates invitations and responses · Produces polished presentations with guidance
  • unfamiliarActivities: Paid employment · Independent budgeting · Public transport alone · Sustained self-directed projects
  • motivations: Belonging to her social circle · Privacy · Maintaining a competent appearance
  • ambitions: Wants to attend college away from home · Has no settled academic interest despite naming impressive options in adult conversations
  • struggles: Difficulty identifying personal preferences · Dependence on structure · Unresolved trust conflict with parents · Social comparison
  • supports: Reliable material support · Teachers who respond quickly · Two close friends
  • practicalConstraints: Strict parental outing rules · Activities shaped by family calendar · Little experience managing everyday responsibilities independently

Still uncertain: What would she choose without a friend or parent selecting the initial options? · Which demonstrated strengths transfer when tutoring and reminders decrease? · Will distance from home clarify her interests or mainly relieve conflict?
